beliefs.limiting: I’ve been drinking for years. I’m stuck with it.
beliefs.counterpart: Most people hooked on alcohol get free in the end. I’m doing it now.
beliefs.test: This week, list everyone you know who used to drink hard and doesn’t now. Ask one of them how stuck they felt before they stopped. Notice whether they once thought what you think now.
beliefs.proof: In a big US survey, 2,008 of 4,781 people ever hooked on alcohol were already free when asked. A projected 90.6% get free in their lifetime.

refs.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.
refs.quote: The subsamples of individuals with life-time DSM-IV diagnosis of dependence on … alcohol (n = 4781)

refs.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.

Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.
refs.quote: Life-time cumulative probability estimates of dependence remission were … 90.6% for alcohol

beliefs.origin: 06-template.json alcohol belief 4 (marked Keep). Limiting and counterpart word for word. Proof changed: the counted figure (2,008 of 4,781 already free, Table 3 of the paper) now goes before the projection (rule 10); 'half within about 14 years' dropped, because that is the who-years kind, a projection not picked in kinds.json.

problems: Holds. The abstract gives n = 4,781 with lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence (NESARC 2001–2002, n = 43,093, face-to-face interviews) and a lifetime cumulative remission probability of 90.6%, made by the actuarial method. The paper calls these 'projections', and the proof says 'projected'. The counted figure comes first (rule 10). Severity 'dependent' fits. The proof is 26 words, with no other addiction named and no cheering.

Minor, no change needed. Table 3 has the column heading 'Alcohol remission (N=2,008)' but never defines N. Reading it as the unweighted count of people who had remitted by the interview is the standard reading for a discrete-time survival table, and it fits the other columns (cannabis 344 of 530, cocaine 336 of 408). The text itself never says '2,008 remitted'.

Minor, no change needed. In this paper 'free' means they had stopped having any dependence symptoms for good ('finally stopped … never started happening again'). They had not necessarily stopped drinking.
All three quotes are word for word, with ellipses that drop the other substances: the first and third from the abstract, the second from the Table 3 heading.

beliefs.limiting: I’ve tried to stop before. I always go back.
beliefs.counterpart: Each try showed me where it breaks. I know more now than I did the first time.
beliefs.test: Write down your last serious try: how long it lasted and the moment it ended. Notice whether that moment was a day, a place or a person you can plan for.
beliefs.proof: Of US adults who beat a drinking or drug problem after at least one serious try, half needed 3 tries or more. The number of tries did not differ significantly by main drug.

refs.cite: Kelly JF, Greene MC, Bergman BG, White WL, Hoeppner BB (2019). How many recovery attempts does it take to successfully resolve an alcohol or drug problem? Estimates and correlates from a national study of recovering U.S. adults. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.
refs.quote: among participants reporting at least 1 serious recovery attempt (n = 1,742), the mean and median number of recovery attempts were slightly higher—6.14 (SD = 14.20) and 3

refs.cite: Kelly JF, Greene MC, Bergman BG, White WL, Hoeppner BB (2019). How many recovery attempts does it take to successfully resolve an alcohol or drug problem? Estimates and correlates from a national study of recovering U.S. adults. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.
refs.quote: there were apparent differences in the distribution of number of recovery attempts by primary substance; however, these did not reach statistical significance

beliefs.origin: new. The group mixes alcohol and drugs (rule 13: said in the proof); the paper reports no difference by main substance. 1,742 people, of 2,002 who resolved a problem.

problems: 'The number of tries did not differ by main drug' is stronger than the paper's results. The abstract sentence is word for word, but the results say there 'were apparent differences … by primary substance; however, these did not reach statistical significance'. Table 1 medians are 2 for alcohol, cannabis and stimulants, 3 for opioids and 1 for other drugs.

The rest holds. Among the n = 1,742 (of 2,002 who resolved a problem) with at least 1 serious try, the median was 3 (IQR 1 to 5), so 'half needed 3 tries or more' is right. The survey is US, 2016, cross-sectional and based on recall, and each person decided what counted as 'serious'. Severity 'resolved' fits. The group mixes drugs, and the proof says so (rule 13). The quote is 28 words, word for word.

Minor, no change needed. Counting everyone, including people with no serious try, the median for people whose main drug was alcohol was 2 (IQR 1 to 4). The paper does not give an alcohol-only median among people with at least one try.

beliefs.limiting: Stopping will be hell. I won’t get through it.
beliefs.counterpart: I’ve got through hard weeks before. This is a few hard weeks, not a hard life.
beliefs.test: Write how hard you think quitting will be, 0 to 10. One evening this week, wait 20 minutes before the first drink and rate the urge every 5 minutes. Notice whether it reached your number, and whether it stayed there.
beliefs.proof: Withdrawal typically starts within a day; mild, low-risk cases are unlikely to turn severe after 36 hours of observation. In 191 inpatient men without earlier major mental illness, serious low mood fell from 42% to 6% by week 4.

refs.cite: American Society of Addiction Medicine (2020). The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management. Journal of Addiction Medicine.
refs.quote: Signs and symptoms of alcohol withdrawal typically begin 6–24 hours after cessation of (or reduction in) alcohol use.

refs.cite: American Society of Addiction Medicine (2020). The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management. Journal of Addiction Medicine.
refs.quote: Patients with mild withdrawal and low risk of complicated withdrawal may be observed for up to 36 hours, after which more severe withdrawal is unlikely to develop.

refs.cite: Brown SA, Schuckit MA (1988). Changes in depression among abstinent alcoholics. Journal of Studies on Alcohol.
refs.quote: depressive symptoms among male primary alcoholics (no preexisting major psychiatric disorder) were studied throughout inpatient treatment for alcoholism. A sample of 191 alcoholics was interviewed

refs.cite: Brown SA, Schuckit MA (1988). Changes in depression among abstinent alcoholics. Journal of Studies on Alcohol.
refs.quote: 42% of alcoholics have clinically significant levels of depression … at intake but only 6% remain clinically depressed at Week 4

beliefs.origin: new (the template had no 'unbearable' row). Answers it with how long alcohol withdrawal lasts; the timeline carries the longer tail (sleep, months).

problems: The ASAM line drops a condition and moves the clock. The guideline says 'Patients with mild withdrawal and low risk of complicated withdrawal may be observed for up to 36 hours, after which more severe withdrawal is unlikely to develop'. That is 36 hours of observation, for patients who are both mild and low risk. The proof leaves out 'low risk', and its wording reads as 36 hours after the last drink.
The '6–24 hours' onset in the guideline applies to withdrawal in general, not only to mild cases. It says 'typically'.

The Brown and Schuckit sample was 'male primary alcoholics (no preexisting major psychiatric disorder)'. Leaving that out makes the drop from 42% to 6% look as if it applies to everyone. The figures (Hamilton score of 20 or more, 42% at intake, 6% at week 4, n = 191 inpatients) are word for word in the abstract. The abstract does not say whether all 191 were still there at week 4, and the full text (J Stud Alcohol 1988) could not be fetched.

Both ASAM quotes are word for word (PDF p. 'Recommendation V.1' and the risk-assessment section), and both Brown and Schuckit quotes are word for word in the abstract. Severity 'treatment' fits both sources. The corrected proof is 40 words (at the limit).

beliefs.limiting: I need a drink to unwind after work.
beliefs.counterpart: Drinking takes the edge off for an hour. It takes my sleep, and sleep is what would unwind me.
beliefs.test: Drink as you normally do this week. Each morning, write last night’s drinks and rate how rested you feel, 0 to 10. Notice whether the bigger nights bring the worse mornings.
beliefs.proof: In sleep-lab studies of men in treatment for alcoholism, drink did not reliably help them sleep. In most of these studies, they took longer to fall asleep and slept less, both on drinking nights and in withdrawal (review).

refs.cite: Brower KJ (2001). Alcohol's effects on sleep in alcoholics. Alcohol Research & Health.
refs.quote: Several research groups in the 1970s and early 1980s used polysomnography to study the sleep of male alcoholics undergoing inpatient alcoholism treatment, both following alcohol administration and during alcohol withdrawal

refs.cite: Brower KJ (2001). Alcohol's effects on sleep in alcoholics. Alcohol Research & Health.
refs.quote: alcohol is not a reliably effective sedative among alcoholic patients. For example, as discussed earlier, alcohol may prolong sleep latency and decrease total sleep time in alcoholics

refs.cite: Brower KJ (2001). Alcohol's effects on sleep in alcoholics. Alcohol Research & Health.
refs.quote: During both drinking periods and withdrawal, alcoholics commonly experience problems falling asleep and decreased total sleep time.

beliefs.origin: 06-template.json alcohol belief 1. Limiting word for word. Counterpart's first sentence changed: 'Drinking doesn’t take my stress away' is not something he already believes; 'takes the edge off for an hour' is. Its second sentence is kept. Proof changed from '5–9 months to fall asleep normally' (a cost of quitting, not of drinking) to what drink does to sleep while drinking.

problems: 'Nights of drinking and of withdrawal both meant trouble falling asleep and less sleep overall' is stronger than the review. The review says alcoholics 'commonly experience' these problems, and that alcohol 'may prolong sleep latency'. It also says this happened 'In most of these studies'; one study (Allen 1980) found more total sleep after alcohol. Skoloda 1979 found that drink briefly improved sleep quality, mainly in the first week.

The rest holds. The studies were polysomnography studies from the 1970s and early 1980s, of male alcoholics in inpatient treatment, done after alcohol was given and during withdrawal. 'Not a reliably effective sedative among alcoholic patients' is in the source. Severity 'treatment' fits. All three quotes are word for word and 30 words or fewer (the first is exactly 30).
Weak, for the card: the studies are old and small, and the review gives no total n.

beliefs.limiting: I’ve got it under control now. I can handle just one.
beliefs.counterpart: I’ve tried “just one” before. I know where it went.
beliefs.test: Write down the last three times you meant to have just one or two. Next to each, write how many it became and how the next day went. Notice how many stayed at one.
beliefs.proof: In a US survey of people who had got free of alcohol dependence, signs of a drinking problem came back within 3 years for 27% of those who drank within low-risk limits, and 7% of those who didn’t drink.

refs.cite: Dawson DA, Goldstein RB, Grant BF (2007). Rates and correlates of relapse among individuals in remission from DSM-IV alcohol dependence: a 3-year follow-up. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.
refs.quote: The Wave 1 NESARC identified 2,109 individuals who met the DSM-IV criteria for full remission from alcohol dependence. Of these, 1,772 were reinterviewed at Wave 2

refs.cite: Dawson DA, Goldstein RB, Grant BF (2007). Rates and correlates of relapse among individuals in remission from DSM-IV alcohol dependence: a 3-year follow-up. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.
refs.quote: By Wave 2, 51.0% of the Wave 1 asymptomatic risk drinkers had experienced the recurrence of AUD symptoms, compared with 27.2% of low-risk drinkers and 7.3% of abstainers.

beliefs.origin: new (rule 4 model). Counts only people who had been dependent and were fully free at the first interview (1,772 re-interviewed). A survey, not a trial: people chose to drink lightly or not at all.

problems: 'Those who drank lightly' is wrong about the group. The source's group is 'low-risk drinkers'. In the same authors' NESARC definitions (Dawson 2005/2006, PMC6527249), a low-risk drinker is a past-year drinker with no abuse or dependence symptoms who stayed under the risk limits. For men that means no more than 14 drinks a week on average and never 5 or more in a day. That is up to 4 a day, not 'just one', and 'lightly' hides this from a reader weighing moderation.

The rest holds. People in full remission from DSM-IV alcohol dependence at Wave 1 (2,109 in 2001–2002) were re-interviewed at Wave 2 in 2004–2005 (1,772). By then any AUD symptoms had come back for 27.2% of low-risk drinkers and 7.3% of abstainers, rounded correctly. Severity 'dependent' fits rule 4. Both quotes are word for word and 30 words or fewer. The corrected proof is 39 words.

Minor, no change needed. 'Signs of a drinking problem' is the recurrence of any AUD symptom. Full dependence came back for 4.0% of low-risk drinkers and 2.9% of abstainers, a much smaller gap. The adjusted odds ratio was 5.8 for any symptom. Age changed the result: for younger alcoholics, the type of remission made no significant difference.
The per-group n behind 27.2% and 7.3% is not in the abstract, and the full text is behind a paywall.

do: Don’t stop yet. For the next few days, drink as you normally do, and watch it.
Write down what drinking does for you: unwinding, sleep, confidence, fun with friends.
Before each drink, note the time, the place and what you want from it. Next morning, note whether you got it.
Allow it. No guilt and no promises this week. You’re finding out, not judging.
Look at each reason up close: does drinking give you that, or take it back by morning?
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Unwinding: a walk, a shower, a hard workout, a show.
Going out: an alcohol-free beer in your hand, ordered first, before anyone asks.
Friends: see the ones you’d enjoy sober; meet them for food, sport or coffee.
Sleep: same bedtime every night, a hot shower, no phone in bed. Expect light sleep at first; it mends over months.
Confidence: arrive early, before the room fills, and start one conversation while you’re fresh.
Home: keep a cold soft drink you like in the fridge for the hour you’d pour one.
Clear the house of drink the day before.
Tell one person the date.
Plan every Friday for the first two months. That’s where the pull lives.
Drinking heavily every day? See a doctor before you stop.
One thing only. No new diet, no gym plan, no other big change for these three months.
Slip? Don’t wait for Monday. Go back to step 1 the same day: what did that drink give you?

proof.text: In a lab test of men treated as inpatients for alcohol, the pull of drink cues was strongest at day 60, the last check, not in week 1.

ref.cite: Li P, Wu P, Xin X, Fan YL, Wang GB, Wang F, Ma MY, Xue MM, Luo YX, Yang FD, Bao YP, Shi J, Sun HQ, Lu L (2015). Incubation of alcohol craving during abstinence in patients with alcohol dependence. Addiction Biology.
ref.quote: inpatient adult male alcoholics … Cue-induced alcohol craving measured with visual analogue scales was the highest at 60 days of abstinence

problems: Holds. The study tested inpatient adult male alcoholics for cue-induced craving at 7, 14, 30 and 60 days of abstinence, both between groups and within one group of 19. Craving rated on visual analogue scales 'was the highest at 60 days of abstinence both between and within groups'. Day 60 was the last check, and the proof says so (rule 19). The quote is word for word with an ellipsis. The proof is 28 words.

Minor, no change needed. Heart rate, blood pressure and skin conductance did not differ between the abstinence groups, so 'pull' means self-rated craving only, which is what the proof describes. The study was in China (not stated in the proof).

do: When “just one” comes, answer the way a non-drinker would: “I don’t drink.”
When the urge comes, name it: “there is a craving.” Not “I want a drink.” Not “I need one.”
Then watch it like weather. Notice when it peaks and when it fades.
Feel fine and think “maybe it wasn’t that bad”? That’s the quitting working, not proof you never had to.
Unsure what to do? Ask what the man a year sober would do tonight, and do that.
Count the mornings you wake up clear, not the days you missed.
Ask a doctor about acamprosate or naltrexone.
Try AA or another group that meets weekly.
Use help as a tool for a stretch, not a new identity. Keep what works, drop the rest.
Ask one friend to check in with you on Fridays for the first two months.
Slipped more than once? Add one kind of help you haven’t tried, then go back to step 1.

proof.text: In trials, for every 12 people who took acamprosate, one more stayed off drink than on a dummy pill.

ref.cite: Jonas DE, Amick HR, Feltner C, et al. (2014). Pharmacotherapy for adults with alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA.
ref.quote: The NNT to prevent return to any drinking for acamprosate was 12

problems: Holds. In a JAMA 2014 meta-analysis of RCTs of 12 weeks or more in outpatient settings (acamprosate: 27 studies, n = 7,519), the NNT to prevent return to any drinking for acamprosate was 12 (95% CI 8 to 26). 'For every 12 … one more stayed off drink than on a dummy pill' is a faithful plain reading. The quote is word for word. The proof is 18 words.
Minor, no change needed. The NNT runs over each trial's own follow-up, not for life.
